heading: Memorandum (to President Hassan, from Team 2422054)
note: 16 blocks, 231 words. The memo is printed at the front of the paper (p2), ahead of the table of contents — the only one of the type-F papers read so far where the memo precedes the abstract sheet's keyword line rather than closing the document. 10 is the To/From/Date/Subject header; 11 announces the list of measures and 12-17 are five bullets, of which the third is split by the line break at 14/15 ('...steadily increasing it at an annual GDP' + 'growth rate over five years'). 18 announces the returns and 19-24 are three return bullets, the economic one spanning 20-22 ('...The potential to' + 'achieve a middle developed country level within 30 years...') and the environmentalist one spanning 23-24. Two numeric defects: the memo promises 'a 47.5% increase in salaries over 5 years', which appears nowhere in the body — block 201 reports +29.5% for the high-income group and +57.5% for the low-income group, whose mean is 43.5%, not 47.5; and the five measures here are seven in the body's own summary at block 71 (tourism and visa-free are folded into one bullet, and the customs-oversight and international-appeal items are compressed into the last bullet). The 28.1% annual IWT reduction and the 16-year elimination do reproduce block 199 and block 201. 25 closes the memo and its tail carries the whole Contents page: 'Memorandum 2 ... 1 Introduction 4 ...'.

heading: 1 Introduction (1.1 Background and Restatement, 1.2 Client Introduction, 1.3 Our Work)
note: 9 blocks, 629 words. The '1 Introduction' and '1.1 Background and Restatement' headings ride in the tail of block 32, the last contents line, and the statement of the three questions the paper answers ('who is the client? What can the client realistically do? Why the project is suitable') is truncated in block 34's extraction, which also swallows the '1.2 Client Introduction' heading. 33 is the only background paragraph and carries no number at all; the paper's first quantitative claims arrive in 48 (1.52 million tourists, tourism at 3.5% of GDP, both 'according to the World Bank') and neither is a reference entry — the list at 241-267 has 27 items and no World Bank source. 35 picks Tanzania as the client and states the three criteria (power, resources, interest) that 36-38 then justify one apiece: presidential system and a long-ruling majority party, fiscal revenue plus hydroelectric supply, and Operation TOKOMEZA. 38 is the citation defect of the introduction: the quotation 'it is also an example of what can be achieved by the men and women of Tanzania committed to protecting the nation' is attributed to [12], which is Hauenstein et al. on elephant poaching rates correlating with poverty — a data paper, not a source for a government statement. 39-40 convert the three criteria into a verdict and 41 announces Figure 1, whose caption is block 44 on the following page; 41's tail also carries '2 Project and Assumptions 2.1 Project Policies', so this chapter ends on a heading that belongs to the next one.

heading: 2 Project and Assumptions (2.1 Project Policies, 2.2 Assumptions and Justification)
note: 40 blocks, 752 words, and 40 printed blocks for 752 words is the paper's structural tell: seven policy bullets are set as separate paragraphs and the extraction cuts every one of them at a line break. 42 is the literature frame and 43+45 is one sentence interrupted by the Figure 1 float ('...can often be categorized as' + 'economic, recreational and traditional [20].'); 44 is the caption ('Figure 1: The Framework of Our Study'). 46 cites the Namibia CBNRM study [21] and the ivory-trade studies [14] to argue that corruption and poverty matter more than poaching bans — a claim the paper then does not use, because all seven of its policies are supply-side or demand-side controls, none is an anti-corruption or poverty measure. 48 supplies the tourism numbers with no reference. Then the instrument list: 49-51 visa waivers, 52-56 agricultural subsidy (five blocks for one bullet), 57-59 infrastructure, 61-63 gun control ('banning the sale of hunting rifles and large-caliber firearms to individuals'), 64-67 customs/immigration/logistics oversight, 68-70 an international appeal. 67 and 70 both assert zero cost ('such oversight will not incur additional costs', 'such an appeal would not entail additional costs') with no budget line behind it, and the government model at 193-194 has exactly two spending instruments (infrastructure and subsidy), so these two free policies are never represented in the optimisation. 71 restates seven policies and promises 'the costs and results of which will be analyzed in more detail later' — the costs are never computed. 72 is the 2.2 heading as its own block (watermarks only otherwise), 73 is the lead, and 74-75, 76-77, 78-81 are the three 'assumptions', each a bullet split across 2-4 blocks; 81's tail carries '3 Data and Notations'.

heading: 3 Data and Notations (3.1 Data Collection and Pre-processing)
note: 11 blocks (82-91 plus the Figure 2 caption at 100, which floats a page and a half later), 421 words plus the caption. 82 is a bare heading. 83-84 obtain CITES trade records and describe CITES with [4]; 84 concedes the raw data are 'constrained by inconsistency in units and lack of sorting'. 85-86 are the minimax normalisation, equation (1), split as 'Xij − min(Xj) Yij = (1)' / 'max(Xj) − min(Xj) where Xij represents...' — the denominator of the printed fraction is separated from its numerator by a page-flow break. 87-88 are equations (2) and (3) (pij = Yij/ΣYij, then the entropy Ej), with 88 carrying the stray 'ln n i=1' fragment of the summation limits. 89-90 give equation (4), Wj = (1−Ej)/(n − ΣEj), after the sentence 'The greater the information entropy, the more significant the term is to the IWT and the greater the weight'. 91 sums the weighted terms into an annual IWTI and says the series is plotted by animal and plant terms in Fig.2 — 100 is that caption, 'Index of IWT in TZA'. The defect that matters: the IWTI is constructed here, plotted once, and then never appears again in the paper. The behavioural model at 101-133 uses λw, λp, βt, Pb, Pw, Lw and wages; the government model at 173-197 uses P_IWT, E[Q_IWT], ΔC, ΔI, ΔG. No equation after 91 contains IWTI, the trade volume that was normalised in 85 is never used as a level, and no numerical value of IWTI is printed anywhere — the only surviving evidence of the index is one figure.

heading: 3.2 Notations (Table 1)
note: 7 blocks, 254 words, of which block 96 alone is 180 'words' of table cells. 92 is the one-sentence lead and its tail carries '4 IWTers' Behavioral Decision Model 4.1 Model Derivation and assumptions'. The table then floats to p10 and p11 and is split into four measured blocks — 94 the caption ('Table 1: Notations used in this paper'), 95 the column header ('Symbol Description Value and Source'), 96 every row, 97 the footnote ('*Some variables are not listed here and will be discussed in detail in each section.') — with 98 and 99 being page-top watermark slivers on p10/p11 (0 and 1 words). Two defects in the rows of 96: the symbol column is shifted by one against the body, so βt is labelled 'The number of wild life appearances per hour 0.4(estimated)' and λw 'The number of police appearances per hour 0.02(estimated)', whereas block 126 defines βt as the transportation cost per hour and λw / λp as the wildlife and police arrival rates — the body's own equation (5) uses βt as a money-per-hour price (Ct = ti·βt); and the row for the transportation cost per hour has a description ('The transportation cost per hour 4.5 dollars') with no symbol at all, so the 4.5 USD/h that equation (5) needs has no variable name. The final row's value, '3.9([10])', is left without a symbol too. Every one of these values is either 'estimated' or a vendor web page ([16] guns, [13] car, [27] weapon lifespan) — there is no Tanzanian micro-data anywhere in the calibration.

heading: 4 IWTers' Behavioral Decision Model (4.1 Model Derivation and Assumptions)
note: 34 blocks, 980 words — the paper's longest chapter, and the one where the block count is inflated by a page break: 93 ('In previous micro-level studies on illegal wildlife traders... despite the often insufficient randomness in the models [6], it was consistently found that the conditions') and 101 ('driving IWT behaviors were, in fact, when the net revenue from illegal wildlife trading exceeded the net revenue from conservation efforts.') are one printed paragraph split by Table 1 and the Figure 2 caption. 102-103 split the cost and the revenue definitions; 104 announces assumptions; 105-107 (car depreciation with fixed lifespan), 108-109 (one weapon, one price, depreciation by rounds fired), 110-113 (high/low-income split plus 'Once arrested, the IWTer faces a period of unemployment, the individual will not experience discrimination in employment upon release'), 114 (Poisson arrivals of animals), 115-117 (Poisson arrivals of law enforcement, arrest on arrival), 118-119 (linear negative price-quantity), 120 (each IWTer does not affect total wildlife), 121-122 (nor the international supply) are eight bullets, each cut at a line break. The model: (5) Ct = ti·βt, (6) Cw = λw·ti·Pb + λw·ti·Pw/Lw, (7) Co = wi·ti + Tp·wi·(1 − e^{−λp·ti}), then (8) PIWT = a − b·λw·ti·e^{−λp·ti} and (9) Ri = λw·ti·PIWT·e^{−λp·ti}. Two substantive errors. First, equation (6) charges bullets at the wildlife-arrival rate λw rather than at a kill rate, so a trader who fires at every animal he meets spends λw·ti rounds, which is the same rate that equation (8) uses to set the quantity supplied — the two uses are never separated and no kill probability exists in the model. Second, the survival probability e^{−λp·ti} enters twice: the quantity λw·ti·e^{−λp·ti} already carries it inside PIWT at (8), and (9) multiplies the revenue by it again, so revenue falls as e^{−2λp·ti} in arrest risk while the cost side at (7) uses only (1 − e^{−λp·ti}) once. 126 defines Tp as 'the time the IWTer spend in prison each month' but (7) prices it as Tp·wi, i.e. as hours forfeited, and never connects it to the arrest probability that would determine how many prison-months occur. 131-132 give the maximisation and the closed form 'ti = Max{0, −53·wi + 20}' with the sentence 'After substituting the approximations and parameters mentioned in the Notation section' — but Table 1's values (βt = 4.5 USD/h, Pb = 1, Pw = 400, Lw = 30000, λw = 0.4, λp = 0.02, and the 3.9 that has no symbol) contain no a, no b, no Tp and no wage level, so neither 53 nor 20 can be reproduced from the printed table; the substitution step is not shown anywhere. 133 reads the sign of the coefficient as the whole result: higher wage, fewer hours.

heading: 4.2 Impact of Policies on Economic Incentives and Recreational Demand
note: 21 blocks, 288 words — 21 printed blocks carrying 288 words, i.e. an average of 14 words per block, because every bullet is broken at a line boundary (136-138, 139-140, 141-142, 143-145, 146-148, 150-152, 153-154). The argument is entirely qualitative: no number appears in the chapter. 135 opens the economic-incentive half and the five bullets say that infrastructure and subsidy raise wages and therefore cut IWT hours, that gun control raises weapon cost, that tighter trade regulation raises the chance of interdiction, and that international appeals cut demand with [24] (Sosnowski et al. on ivory prices since the 1989 CITES ban — a price series, offered as evidence of a demand decline). 149 opens the recreational half and the two bullets argue that poaching is substitutable with travel, video games and basketball [11], and that rebellion poaching is displaced when basic needs are met [5]. The last two bullets are the ones the model cannot absorb: the model's only micro variable is monthly hours ti driven by wage wi, so 'recreational motives' and 'symbol of rebellion' enter as an assertion that the same wage channel covers them, with no term in equations (5)-(11) for either, and the reference for leisure substitutability is a conceptual paper on the leisure-substitution concept rather than evidence about poachers.

heading: 5 Government's Political Decision Model (opening, 5.1 lead)
note: 18 blocks, 273 words. 155 is the bare chapter head; 156 sets the three goals (prevent IWT, promote growth, ensure distributive equity) and says 'we believe the core objectives of the government should include' — the goals are asserted, not sourced from any Tanzanian policy document. 157 announces assumptions and 158-172 are five bullets: three objectives only and unquantifiable secondary ones excluded (158-160), GDP as C + I + G with net exports dropped 'due to its small share' (161-162), consumption linear in household income with the effect varying by group and 'the effect is linearly uncorrelated' (163-165 — the phrase is self-contradictory as printed: a linear and positive correlation whose magnitude varies across groups is not the same claim as 'linearly uncorrelated'), universal infrastructure investment with heterogeneous effects while the agricultural subsidy hits only the low-income group, the two being 'linearly separable' for that group (166-170), and a constant GDP share spent on both instruments (171-172). 172's tail carries '5.1 Model Derivation'. Net exports are dropped as small while tourism — the paper's own first policy, and the only one with a GDP number attached at 48 — is a service export, so the assumption removes from the model the channel the paper most wants to claim.

heading: 5.1 Model Derivation
note: 27 blocks, 1139 words. 173 leads into (12) Ggov = a1·GIWT + a2·GGDP + a3·Gequ with Σai = 1 (174-176, the summation limits split onto their own line at 175). 177 is the two-panel Figure 3 caption ('Goals of the Government of TZA' / 'Structures of Tanzania GDP') — a figure whose structure the text never reads. 178-182 define GIWT = −PIWT·E[QIWT] with (13) E[QIWT] = 12·λw·t·e^{−λp·t} and (15) t = plow·tlow + (1 − plow)·thigh; 179 and 181 each carry two numbered equations whose numbers land on the following block, so (13)/(14) and (15) are physically split. 183-186 build GGDP from the expenditure approach with [22] and [25], (16) GGDP = wc·ΔC + wi·ΔI + wg·ΔG. 187 states the distributional assumptions and 188-189 give (17)-(19). 190-192 give (20)/(21), Δwlow = [(1 − c4)·ΔInv]·c5 + ΔSub·c6 and its high-income twin, with c5 forced equal across both groups by assumption. 193-194 are the budget constraint, checked against the rendered page 17: it is printed as one two-line display, (22) Bt = Bt−1 + ΔGDPt−1 and (23) = Bt−1 + ρ(ΔInfrat + ΔSubt), with ρ introduced in the prose at 193 as 'the proportion of additional spending,ρ, that the government is willing to provide' and never listed in Table 1 — so every instrument is paid for out of last year's growth increment and nothing can be funded from a standing budget in year one. Equation (22) as printed also subtracts a budget from a budget and equates it to a GDP increment, which mixes a stock with a flow. 195-197 give (24) Gequ = Δwlow/Δwhigh — its lead sentence reads 'comparing the income changes between low high-income groups', a dropped word — and the objective max Infra Ggov (25). The weights a1, a2, a3 are introduced at (12) and never assigned in this chapter: the values 0.2, 0.6, 0.2 first appear at block 204, inside the sensitivity section, described as 'the previous model'. 198 announces the numerical refinement and a 30-year horizon; 199 delivers the headline, 'illegal wildlife trade can be completely eradicated within 16 years', and its tail carries the truncated '5.2 Short-sighted Government' heading as the fragment '…… Government'.

heading: 5.2 Short-sighted Government
note: 3 blocks, 145 words. 200 explains the section's purpose (short-term effects to survive electoral rotation). 201 is the only place where the five-year outcome is quantified in the body: 'without accounting for inflation, the hourly wage of the high-income group and the low-income group will increase by 29.5% and 57.5%, and the annual illegal wildlife trade will decrease by 28.1% as planned', referred to Table 2 — which is where the evidence should be, and Table 2 is unreadable in the extracted text: blocks 239-240 preserve only the column header 'Period Project GDP Wage_High Wage_Low IWT Infrastructure (1e+12 TZS) (TZS/h) (TZS/h)' and two stray values, '4139.969 0' and '935.682', with the caption 'Table 2: The Optimal Decision and Prediction' arriving after them. So a single sentence in 201 and two orphaned numbers are the entire quantitative output of a 30-year optimisation. 202 asserts 'a increasing future marginal trend ... both in the salary increase and illegal wildlife trade reduction' with no series to support it.

heading: 6 Sensitivity Analysis (6.1 Weight-specific, 6.2 Policy-specific)
note: 6 blocks, 437 words. 203 is the bare 6.1 head. 204 is where the objective weights finally appear — 'weights of 0.2, 0.6, and 0.2 were assigned ... This suggests that the Tanzanian government is focused on economics more' — and it is the only sensitivity run whose result is stated in words ('our polices lead to consistent growth over the next 30 years'), with the numbers cut off by the extraction at 'Especially, IW'. No alternative weight vector is reported: a weight-specific analysis that prints one weight set and one qualitative outcome is a statement of the baseline, not a sensitivity analysis. 205 is the 6.2 lead, 206 the caption 'Figure 4: Sensitivity of Policy Change', 207 sets the ±10% band on implementation of the two instruments, and 208 reads the four panels purely qualitatively ('wildlife conservation is the most robust of the three main goals', 'relatively robust to policy changes without significant fluctuations'). Not one perturbed value is tabulated, so the claim of robustness rests on the reader's reading of a four-panel figure.

heading: 7 Policy Impacts in a Larger Complex System (7.1 IWT and Climate Change, 7.2 IWT and Other Forms of Trafficking)
note: 11 blocks, 520 words; '8 Strengths and Weaknesses 8.1 Strengths' rides in 219's tail. This chapter adds no model — it is three paragraphs of climate argument and four of crime-linkage argument, all unquantified. 213 carries the load-bearing claim: 'protecting and restoring wildlife can enhance natural carbon capture and sequestration, even capturing up to 95% of the carbon needed to achieve goals of The Paris Agreement each year[23]' — the paper converts a global natural-climate-solutions estimate into a benefit of Tanzanian anti-poaching policy with no scaling, no baseline, and no share of Tanzanian wildlife in the 95%. 214 cites 'IPBE and IPCC' (IPBES is misspelled) for the biodiversity-climate link. 212 asserts that reducing IWT cuts transport emissions, though the model's transport cost is a per-hour car price and never a quantity of freight. 215-218 give four mechanisms by which IWT intertwines with drugs and arms (combination concealment, shared smuggling routes, barter, funding), and 219 supplies the number: 'IWT worth up to $213 billion dollars a year is funding organized crime, including global terror groups and militias[17]' — a Guardian report on IWT and charcoal trade, an order of magnitude above the CITES-scale estimates the paper's own data source would support, and never reconciled with the IWTI series built in chapter 3.

heading: 8 Strengths and Weaknesses (8.1 Strengths, 8.2 Weaknesses)
note: 17 blocks, 217 words — four strength bullets of 3-5 blocks each and one 33-word weakness. 220-224 claim innovation from iterating micro and macro models; 225-228 claim flexibility because randomness is included ('Despite not having access to a complete data distribution'); 229-232 claim theoretical rigour; 233-235 claim stability because the model 'has undergone rigorous sensitivity testing'. 236 is the entire weaknesses section: 'In parameter estimation, due to the unavailability of micro-level data from reputable institutions in Tanzania, we relied on data from the Tanzanian internet or information sources, which may introduce biased estimates.' The admitted weakness is decisive and is not carried into the conclusion or the memo: the two behavioural parameters that drive the whole result (53 and 20 in equation (11)) come from no printed substitution, and the elasticity that produces the 28.1% is therefore not attributable to data at all. The asymmetry — four claims of strength, one sentence of weakness, no stated limitation of the objective function's 0.2/0.6/0.2 weights — is the chapter's structural finding.

heading: 9 Conclusion (with Table 2)
note: 4 blocks, 179 words, and the last of them is almost entirely a broken table. 237-238 restate the two-model structure; 239 closes the prose ('Protecting wildlife is crucial not only for ethical reasons but also for our own survival') and then the table that the conclusion depends on begins inside the same extracted block — 'Period Project GDP Wage_High Wage_Low IWT Infrastructure (1e+12 TZS) (TZS/h) (TZS/h) …… 4139.969 0' — and 240 finishes it with '935.682 Table 2: The Optimal Decision and Prediction'. So the caption is printed after the fragment, the 30-year path is not recoverable from the extracted text, and every number the paper sells to the client (the 16-year eradication, the 28.1%, the 29.5%/57.5% wage gains) rests on a table whose contents do not survive. No policy recommendation chapter is present: the recommendations live only in the memo at the front and in the instrument list at 42-71.
